result.markdown: --- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.bipartite_minimum_weight_full_matching()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: >- Solve the assignment problem: a minimum-weight full matching of a bipartite graph. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.bipartite_minimum_weight_full_matching()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: >- Solve the assignment problem: a minimum-weight full matching of a bipartite graph. title: >- [Graph.bipartite_minimum_weight_full_matching()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: >- Solve the assignment problem: a minimum-weight full matching of a bipartite graph. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Solve the assignment problem: a minimum-weight full matching of a bipartite graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L66446-L66533){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.bipartite_minimum_weight_full_matching( top_nodes=None, weighted=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Bipartite minimum weight full matching](/assets/graphs/bipartite-minimum-weight-full-matching.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Three couriers, Ana, Ben, and Cho, in a column on the left, every one linked to three deliveries d1, d2, d3 on the right. The cheapest assignment, in the accent color, is Ana–d2 (3), Ben–d1 (3), and Cho–d3 (5); the other six links are faded. The table of travel times highlights those three cells and gives the total 3 + 3 + 5 = 11, even though Ana's nearest delivery is d1 (2)." width="100%"} Given two groups, such as workers and tasks, and a cost for each possible pairing (an edge between the groups, weighted by its cost), the assignment problem asks for the cheapest way to give every member of the smaller group a distinct partner from the larger group. Missing edges are pairings that are not allowed. Classic uses include assigning jobs to machines, drivers to ride requests, and tracking objects between video frames. The sides are found by 2-coloring the graph (ignoring edge direction) unless they are given with `top_nodes=`. Every node of the smaller side is matched; on a tie in size, both sides are fully matched. To maximize a total score instead of minimizing a cost, negate the weights. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [top_nodes]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional list of the nodes on one side (IDs or labels); all other nodes form the other side. If `None` (default), the sides are found automatically. [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to use edge weights as costs. If `None` (default), follows the graph's `weighted` flag; with `False` every pairing costs `1`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The IDs of the matched edges, in ascending order. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is not bipartite, `top_nodes=` leaves an edge within one side, or no matching covers the whole smaller side. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The Hungarian method (Kuhn 1955, Munkres 1957) adds the nodes of the smaller side one at a time and grows the matching along a cheapest augmenting path, found with Dijkstra-like scans over reduced costs kept non-negative by node potentials. With $r$ rows (smaller side) and $c$ columns it runs in $O(r^2 c)$ time, the same optimum that NetworkX obtains from SciPy's `linear_sum_assignment`. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Three couriers and three deliveries, with travel times as weights. The quickest assignment is not the one that gives each courier their nearest delivery: ::: {#39adbd6c .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(weighted=True).add_nodes(["Ana", "Ben", "Cho", "d1", "d2", "d3"]) g.add_edges( [ ("Ana", "d1", 2.0), ("Ana", "d2", 3.0), ("Ana", "d3", 8.0), ("Ben", "d1", 3.0), ("Ben", "d2", 7.0), ("Ben", "d3", 9.0), ("Cho", "d1", 6.0), ("Cho", "d2", 4.0), ("Cho", "d3", 5.0), ] ) plan = g.bipartite_minimum_weight_full_matching(top_nodes=["Ana", "Ben", "Cho"]) [ (g.get_label_from_id(e.source), g.get_label_from_id(e.target), e.weight) for e in (g.get_edge(i) for i in plan) ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [('Ana', 'd2', 3.0), ('Ben', 'd1', 3.0), ('Cho', 'd3', 5.0)] ``` ::: ::: The total is 3 + 3 + 5 = 11. Giving Ana her nearest delivery (d1, 2) would leave Ben with d2 or d3 and cost more overall.
